ch01.note: The steel bridge across the mouth of Suzhou Creek where it joins the Huangpu, at the north end of the Bund; in the foreign settlements of the day it was known in English as the Garden Bridge. The whole drive that follows — over the bridge, down the Bund, west along Nanjing Road and out along what the settlement called Bubbling Well Road (the Jing'an Temple Road further on) to the western villa district — traces the real map of the International Settlement in 1930.

The Taishang Ganying Pian (太上感应篇), the “Tract of the Most High on Action and Response,” a short Daoist morality book usually dated to the Song dynasty, which teaches that every good or evil act draws an exact recompense from Heaven. For centuries it was among the most frequently reprinted of all Chinese religious texts, and was commonly printed and given away free as an act of merit, exactly as old Mr. Wu does here. Its best-known couplet is quoted a little further on.

Wenchang Dijun, the Daoist god of literature and of success in the imperial examinations, worshipped above all by the scholar class. The couplet that follows — “of all vices lust is the first, of all virtues filial piety comes first” — is a popular morality maxim of the sort such tracts spread, cited here as the Lord Wenchang's own teaching.

The “reform party” renders weixin dang, the reform current of the late Qing that culminated in the abortive Hundred Days' Reform of 1898; a “reform-party” man was a modernizing reformer. That old Mr. Wu's forebears were shilang (vice-ministers) of the imperial government, while he had once been a reformer and is now a Daoist recluse, sets up the novel's recurring motif of the conflict of the generations.

ch01.anchor: monster the Master would not speak of
ch01.note: An allusion to the Analects (Book VII): “The Master did not speak of prodigies, feats of strength, disorders, or spirits” (zi bu yu). To the old man the motor-car is exactly such an unspeakable prodigy.

Jintong yunü, the boy and girl who attend a Daoist immortal in popular iconography, emblems of unspoiled innocence. Old Mr. Wu casts his young daughter and son in these roles, which makes their swift corruption by Shanghai the sharper.

The crossing of Nanjing Road and Henan Road, long known by this name (literally “the ball-throwing ground,” after a recreation ground once on the spot); one of the busiest intersections of the International Settlement.
Fan Bowen reaches for a bookish classical phrase, shenshen er li, “to revile at length”; the stilted diction is of a piece with the affected poet he is drawn as.
A year in the sexagenary cycle by which years were traditionally reckoned; jiazi is the first of the sixty. The dating places the postscript in 1924.

ch02.note: The Whampoa Military Academy (黄埃军校), founded near Guangzhou in 1924 and headed at its opening by Chiang Kai-shek, trained the officer corps of the National Revolutionary Army; its graduates formed a tight military network, and to be a “Whampoa man” carried the prestige of that origin. Lei Ming and Huang Fen are both of this stamp, which is why each knows the other’s history so well.

Years of the Republic were counted from 1912, so the “sixteenth year” is 1927. Lei is recalling the Northern Expedition’s battles along the Beijing–Hankou (Jinghan) railway that spring, when the Nationalist armies drove north toward Wuhan; the Fourth and Eleventh Armies he names were among its units. The dating quietly measures the present war of 1930 against that earlier, more idealistic campaign, in which Lei fought as a believer.

The war in the background of these chapters is the Central Plains War of 1930, in which Chiang Kai-shek’s Nanjing government (the “Central Army”) fought the allied forces of Feng Yuxiang’s Northwest Army (西北军) and Yan Xishan of Shanxi, who together had set up a rival “Enlarged Conference” government in the north. The swaying fortunes of that fighting are exactly what drive the government-bond market these men live and die by.

The Dragon-Boat Festival (端阳, the fifth day of the fifth lunar month) was one of the three days of the year on which accounts were traditionally settled and debts called in. Its approach is why Zhu Yinqiu’s bankers are pressing him to clear his loans, and why the speculators reckon the coming squeeze against it.

In 1915–16 Yuan Shikai, the Republic’s first president, proclaimed himself emperor under the reign-title Hongxian (洪宪); the monarchy collapsed within months amid nationwide revolt, and Yuan died soon after. The gibe is that Shang Zhongli is just the sort of court literatus — a “literary attendant” (文学佩从), a scholar kept in waiting on a throne — who would have risen under such a monarchy, and who has since had to make his way “from office into trade.”

ch02.anchor: the golden cicada casting its shell
ch02.note: “The golden cicada casts its shell” (金蝉脱壳) is one of the classic Thirty-Six Stratagems: as the insect leaves an intact empty husk behind, one slips free of danger while leaving a convincing semblance in place. Du Zhuzhai suspects the “bull company” is Zhao Botao’s device for sliding his own exposed long position onto his new partners before the reckoning falls due.

ch03.note: “Dance of death” renders si de tiaowu (死的跳舒), the Chinese for the medieval European danse macabre or Totentanz, the allegory in which Death leads off all ranks of society in a dance. Fan Bowen turns the figure against the revelling rich: their gaiety grows the more frenzied as the countryside collapses around them — a doomed carnival on the very edge of the grave.

“Our Mr. Wang” is Wang Jingwei (汪精卫), leader of the Nationalists’ left-leaning Reorganizationist faction, who in 1930 threw in with the northern coalition against Chiang Kai-shek and its rival ‘Enlarged Conference’ government. Tang Yunshan is his man, and the doctrine preached here — that industrial capital should force politics onto the right track — is the faction’s line. See the note on the Enlarged Conference in Chapter Two.

茨立克, the transliteration of Craven “A”, the cork-tipped Virginia cigarette of Carreras Ltd., a fashionable imported brand in the Shanghai of the day — a small, exact marker of Zhu Yinqiu’s standing even as he pleads poverty.

The slang is hu yu zhuyi (潤浴主义), literally ‘bath-ism,’ from the Wu-dialect hu yu, to take a bath. Zhu Yinqiu, who measures every man by himself, decides that Sun Jiren’s grand talk of running enterprises is really a scheme to slip into the warm water and soak at the shareholders’ expense — to feather his own nest under cover of the bank. The exact force of the phrase is now obscure, and the rendering is provisional.

The May Thirtieth Movement (五半运動) began on 30 May 1925, when British-officered police in the Shanghai International Settlement fired on a Chinese demonstration and killed several; the killings set off nationwide strikes, boycotts and anti-imperialist agitation, a founding moment of the mid-1920s revolution. It was against this ferment that the schoolgirl Lin Peiyao first met the young man now returned as Staff Officer Lei.

Goethe’s Die Leiden des jungen Werthers (1774), the novel of hopeless love and suicide that became a cult across Europe; in Chinese Shaonian Weite zhi fannao (《少年維特之烦恼》), celebrated in Guo Moruo’s 1922 version and a byword among May Fourth youth for romantic feeling. That Staff Officer Lei has carried it, with a pressed white rose, through all his campaigns marks him as a man of that generation’s sentiment.

ch04.note: “Local emperor” renders tu huangdi (土皇帝), the stock name for a rural despot who lorded it over his district as a petty sovereign in his own right — the very class of landlord-gentry the peasant movement of these years set out to break.

ch04.anchor: Down with the local bullies and the evil gentry
ch04.note: “Down with the local bullies and the evil gentry” (dadao tuhao lieshen, 打倒土豪劣绳) was the great rallying-cry of the peasant associations of the late-1920s revolution, aimed at exactly Zeng Canghai’s kind. The flag that goes up with it — “the blue sky, the white sun, and the wholly red earth” (青天白日满地红) — is the national flag of the Republic under the Nationalists, so that the new order’s slogan and its banner reach Shuangqiao together.

An earth-peddler (tu fan, 土販) is a dealer in raw opium, tu (“earth”) being the common slang for the drug. The pun a few lines on — “where there was ‘earth’ there was ‘wealth’” — turns on this: Li Si’s swelling power rests on the opium traffic.

The Three Principles of the People (Sanmin zhuyi, 三民主义) — nationalism, democracy, and the people’s livelihood — is the body of doctrine set out by Sun Yat-sen and made the official creed of the Nationalist party and state. The “Premier” to whom Zeng Canghai prays a little later is Sun himself, whom the party revered under that title (zongli). That a rapacious usurer should enshrine the book like a holy relic is the chapter’s sharpest stroke against the new dispensation.

ch04.anchor: Sacred Edict of the old Qing days
ch04.note: The Sacred Edict is the Shengyu Guangxun (圣谋广训, the “Amplified Instructions on the Sacred Edict”), a set of moral maxims issued by the Kangxi and Yongzheng emperors and expounded to the common people at fixed intervals throughout the Qing. Zeng Canghai measures the new party scripture by the old imperial one: to him the Three Principles is simply the Sacred Edict of the present dynasty, an object of compulsory reverence.

Sun Chuanfang (孙传芳, 1885–1935) was the militarist who ruled the five provinces of the lower Yangtze, Shanghai among them, until the Northern Expedition swept him away in 1926–27. To have helped him hunt down and shoot Nationalists is exactly the past that Zeng Canghai, now at the insurgents’ mercy, most needs to disown.

ch05.anchor: better a gap than a makeweight
ch05.note: The maxim is ning que wu lan (宁缺毋滥), “better to leave a place empty than fill it with the unfit.” Wu Sunfu invokes it to justify keeping the weaker capitalists — Zhu Yinqiu, Chen Junyi, Zhou Zhongwei — out of the new combine as partners, even as their factories are marked for “rescue.”

Sun Yat-sen’s Jianguo fanglue (建国方略), a programme for China’s development written 1917–20. Its industrial section proposed a vast “Great Eastern Port” (东方大港) near the mouth of the Yangtze and a national grid of trunk railways; Tang Yunshan, a party man, recites it as scripture. That the plan was still a paper vision in 1930 is the point of Wu Sunfu’s wariness a moment later.

ch05.anchor: Three Fairy Isles upon the sea
ch05.note: The three fabled isles of the immortals — Penglai, Fangzhang and Yingzhou — which old legend set in the eastern sea and which were said to recede as any seeker drew near. The figure casts Sun Yat-sen’s Great Eastern Port and trunk railways as a shimmering mirage, forever promised and never reached.

The quatrain laments the modern spoiling of the West Lake at Hangzhou. The Su Causeway (苏堂) is the willow-planted dyke traditionally credited to the poet Su Shi; the “Lady of the West” renders Xizi (西子), the lake itself, likened ever since Su Shi’s famous couplet to Xi Shi, the great beauty of antiquity. Fan Bowen sets that classical loveliness against the beetle-cars and vulgar villas of the new bourgeoisie.

Fan Bowen’s jibe cuts two ways: in praising the guileless Ah Xuan as more truly “a poet” than a money-god, he means the “Mammon enthroned in his hall of gold” for Wu Sunfu himself, the industrialist in whose house they all sit. Hence the women’s laughter and Wu Sunfu’s scowl — and, a moment later, the barbed question about the silk filature.

Du Xueshi (杜学诗), the sixth of the Du brothers; his given name means literally “study poetry.” Wu Sunfu, who has just sneered at Fan Bowen’s verses, plays on the name — it is Xueshi, “the study of poetry,” who will amount to something — to signal that he would sooner see Peishan matched with the Du brother than with the poet.

ch06.note: Grand Master Qu is Qu Yuan (屈原, c. 340–278 BCE), the poet and loyal minister of the state of Chu who, in despair at his slanderers and his kingdom’s ruin, drowned himself in the Miluo River. In the Fisherman he is pictured wandering and “chanting on the riverbank” (行吟泽碗) — the very phrase Wu Zhisheng turns, a little further on, into the title of Fan Bowen’s imagined poem. To “play Grand Master Qu” is to drown oneself.

An incense-fair (香市) was the crowded spring temple fair held at a local shrine — here the Earth-God Temple (土地庙, the shrine of a locality’s tutelary earth-god) — where worshippers burned incense while pedlars, showmen and performing-animal troupes gathered. It is the one taste of village festivity the sheltered Fourth Young Lady is allowed to remember.
“Doctor of All Trades” renders wanneng boshi (万能博士), literally the “omnipotent” or all-purpose doctor — an ironic title for the dabbler Du Xintuo, who has taken up a dozen studies and finished none.

A follower of Mikhail Bakunin (1814–76), the Russian founder of collectivist anarchism, who preached the abolition of the state. Mao Dun uses the label satirically: Du Xintuo’s “Bakuninism” comes to no more than the pose that “finds nothing to its liking, yet cares about nothing either.”

“The thickest face under heaven” renders tianzi diyi hao (天字第一号), the “number-one, ‘heaven’-class article.” The old Thousand-Character Classic opened with the word “heaven” (天), so “heaven, number one” came to mean the very first or foremost of its kind; a “thick face” (厚脸) is brazen effrontery. Fan Bowen crowns Zeng Jiaju the most shameless man alive.

ch07.note: The Dawes Plan (1924) and the Young Plan (1929), the American-led schemes that rescheduled Germany’s First World War reparations and, in effect, put the recovery of Europe under the direction of United States finance; Charles G. Dawes and Owen D. Young were the American financiers who gave them their names. A “second Dawes Plan” applied to China is Wu Sunfu’s phrase for what Li Yuting has just described — American finance capital dictating terms to a newly unified China, as it had to Weimar Germany.

ch07.anchor: employ no man you doubt, doubt no man you employ
ch07.note: A well-worn maxim, 用人不疑，疑人不用: place complete trust in the men you employ, and do not employ those you cannot trust. Tu Weiyue’s barbed courtesy turns it against his master — by rushing to the mill instead of awaiting the promised telephone call, Wu Sunfu has betrayed that he does not wholly trust the men who serve under him.

The 反间计, the “stratagem of turning the enemy’s agents,” is one of the classic Thirty-Six Stratagems: one feeds the adversary false intelligence through his own informers, or turns them to one’s own use. Tu Weiyue’s plan — to dismiss the secretly bought-over Yao Jinfeng in public, so that the workers rally to her and the go-slow collapses of its own accord — is exactly such a double game.

The Hongmen (洪门) was the great sworn-brotherhood secret society of south China, kin to the Triads and the Elder-Brother Society (哥老会); its members were bound by oath to come to one another’s aid. That pockmarked Li can call up ten-odd “brothers” to break heads at a word marks the mill’s labour politics as an affair of gangs quite as much as of unions.

ch07.anchor: Man's life is like the morning dew
ch07.note: 人生如朝露, “man’s life is like the morning dew” — an image for the brevity of life old in Chinese verse, running from the Book of Han’s tale of Su Wu to Cao Cao’s celebrated line “what is a life? — even as the morning dew” (譬如朝露). On Du Xintuo’s idle lips it is mere aesthetic melancholy; to Wu Sunfu, fresh from the day’s reverses, it falls as an evil omen.

ch08.note: “Smiling tiger” (笑面虎) is the stock Chinese name for a man whose genial face hides a predator’s heart; here it is Feng Yunqing’s settled nickname among the peasants he ruins. Mao Dun sets it beside “flew his kite on a long string” (长线放远鹞), the usurer’s patience that lets a tiny loan ripen, over years, into another man’s land.

To wear the green headscarf (绿头巾) is to be a cuckold. Green was the colour the Yuan and Ming states forced on registered prostitutes and their menfolk, and it fixed itself in the language as the badge of a man whose wife is unfaithful — the same figure that survives in the modern “green hat” (绿帽子). The image threads through the chapter, from the concubine’s nightlife to the turtle scrawled on Feng’s own wall.

ch08.anchor: inviting the gentleman to step into the jar
ch08.note: “Invite the gentleman to step into the jar” (请君入瓮) is to serve a man by the very method he devised for others. In a Tang tale the cruel official Lai Junchen asked his colleague Zhou Xing how to break a stubborn prisoner; Zhou proposed sealing him in a great jar ringed with fire — whereupon Lai produced a warrant for Zhou’s own arrest and said, “Pray, sir, step into the jar.” Feng, who has spent his life snaring peasants, feels himself for once the man in the jar.

He Shen’an quotes the Mencius (1B.5): pressed to practise benevolent government, King Xuan of Qi keeps pleading a private vice — “I have a failing, I am fond of wealth… I have a failing, I am fond of women” (寡人有疾，寡人好色) — and Mencius turns each excuse back into a duty. On He Shen’an’s lips the classical tag becomes a procurer’s cue: Zhao Botao’s known weakness for women is the crack through which they mean to reach him.

“Loosing the pigeon” (放白鸽) and the “immortal’s leap” (仙人跳) are old Shanghai underworld names for a badger-game or marriage swindle, in which a woman is used as bait to entrap and fleece a mark. He Shen’an’s scheme — to dangle Feng’s own daughter before the lecherous Zhao Botao — is exactly such a con, dressed up as a stroke of speculative finance.

“Wife-sharing” (公妻, the communizing of wives) was a stock slander flung at the Communists in these years — the charge that their “communism” would abolish the family and hold women, like property, in common. Feng Yunqing, who has just pandered his own daughter to recoup his losses, turns the propaganda inside out in the chapter’s last line: it is he, in bourgeois Shanghai, who has made his womenfolk common goods.

ch09.note: The May Thirtieth Movement (五卅运动) took its name from 30 May 1925, when police under British command at the Louza Station of the International Settlement fired on a crowd demonstrating on Nanjing Road over the killing of a Chinese worker at a Japanese-owned mill, leaving several dead. The shooting set off a general strike and a wave of anti-imperialist boycotts across China, and its anniversary became a fixed occasion for demonstrations. The scene here is the fifth anniversary, 30 May 1930.

“Three-stripes” (三道头) was Shanghai slang for the British and other Western sergeant-inspectors of the Municipal Police, so called for the chevrons on their sleeves; they ranked above the Chinese and Sikh constables on the beat.

“Red-turbaned Ah-San” (红头阿三) was the common, derisive Shanghai name for the turbaned Sikh constables the British recruited into the Municipal Police from their Indian empire; 阿三, “Number Three,” set them below the Western and Chinese police in the settlement’s racial order.

Fan Bowen adapts a famous couplet by the Tang poet Yuan Zhen (元稹, 779–831): “Having once known the vastness of the sea, one can hardly reckon other waters water” (曾经沧海难为水). Written in mourning for his dead wife, the line had long since passed into a proverb for anything beside which all later things are measured and found wanting.

An allusion to the ancient saying that when King Mu of Zhou marched south his whole army was lost, the gentlemen among them turning into gibbons and cranes, the common soldiers into insects and sand (君子为猿鹤，小人为虫沙). The figure 猿鹤虫沙 came to stand for men killed in war, whatever their rank; Du Xintuo chants it as a cold epitaph on the day’s demonstration.

Diu na ma (丢那妈) is a coarse Cantonese oath; Zhao Botao, a Cantonese, swears in his own dialect. The words that follow it, 寡老, are likewise Cantonese, and their force here is uncertain—probably a rough, jocular form of address rather than a term with a settled meaning.

ch10.note: San Malu (三马路, literally ‘Third Avenue’) is the old colloquial name of Hankou Road (汉口路), the third of the roads running west from the Bund. It was the financial street of Chinese Shanghai, where the Chinese Securities Exchange stood, and so stands here for the bond market itself.

ch10.anchor: put the greater right above kinship
ch10.note: Renders 大义灭亲, a phrase from the Zuo Zhuan: a loyal officer of Wei had his own son put to death for treason, and the chronicler praised him for setting the greater public good above the bond of blood. Li Yuting uses it of pressing Du Zhuzhai to turn against his own brother-in-law Wu Sunfu for the sake of a settlement with Zhao Botao.

Peng Dehuai (彭德怀, 1898–1974), the Communist commander whose Red Army did in fact take Yuezhou and briefly hold Changsha — but in late July 1930, some seven weeks after the fourth of June the novel gives here. Mao Dun compresses the chronology, folding the Red Army’s summer offensive into the same days as the warlord Zhang-Gui armies’ drive on Changsha, so that both alarms strike the bond market at a single stroke.

ch10.anchor: The Lady Ming Goes Out to the Frontier
ch10.note: 明妃出塞, a stock subject of Chinese painting: Wang Zhaojun (王昭君), a palace lady of the Han sent in marriage to the Xiongnu chieftain beyond the Great Wall. Called 明妃, ‘the Lady Ming,’ to avoid the taboo personal name of the Jin emperor Sima Zhao, she became the enduring emblem of a beauty exiled among the barbarians. Here the scene is worked in kesi (缂丝), the fine ‘cut-silk’ tapestry — a costly thing of exile hung, with unconscious irony, in the house of a man who lives by the frontier wars.

By the reckoning of Chinese kinship, Lin Peishan stands a generation above Du Xintuo, though the two are much of an age. Peishan’s elder sister Peiyao is the wife of Wu Sunfu, whose sister is married to Du Zhuzhai, Xintuo’s father; so Peishan ranks as an aunt to Xintuo by marriage. A match that crossed the generation-lines of a family was felt as a grave impropriety, a scrambling of the proper order, which is why the attachment so alarms the elders.

The ‘Hamburg lot,’ the ‘consignment,’ and the ‘goods’ to be run to Yantai (烟台, on the Shandong coast) are a cargo of contraband arms: Tang Yunshan, a partisan of the anti-Nanjing coalition, is smuggling munitions to the northern war-lords for their war on Chiang Kai-shek, and Wu Sunfu is his silent backer. The detail binds Wu Sunfu’s bond speculation to the political gamble on the war’s outcome. 亨堡 is obscure — probably Hamburg, the German port the arms came from, though it may be no more than a cover-word for the shipment; the reading is provisional.

ch11.note: “Rising wind” renders 涨风, the tide-driven gale of the season; but 涨 (zhang, “to rise, to swell”) is also the word for a rising market, so Han Mengxiang’s joke is that Old Zhao, the great bond speculator, loves a “rising wind” of quite another kind — a bull market.

From the proverb 狗咬吕洞宾，不识好人心 (“the dog bites Lü Dongbin, not knowing a good man’s heart”): to repay kindness with hostility, to mistake a friend for a foe. Lü Dongbin is one of the Eight Immortals of Daoist legend.

The “Western Gaol” (西牢) was the prison of the foreign-administered Shanghai International Settlement; a Chinese offender sentenced through the Settlement’s courts might be held there rather than in a Chinese jail.
“Bottom-of-the-chest money” (垫箱钱) is the private nest-egg a bride keeps at the bottom of her trousseau chest — here Feng Meiqing’s own dowry, which her father now means to stake on the bond market.

ch11.anchor: the master of the house shall make his fortune
ch11.note: A folk omen: for a window-blind to be swept up onto the roof was taken as a sign that the household was about to prosper. Feng Yunqing, already primed by prayer and by drawing lots, seizes on the accident as heaven’s confirmation.
